## Personality

Curious, chatty and always muddy. He asks why about everything and remembers every answer.

## Lore

Alaric is nine years old, the younger child of Queen Aveline and Leofric, and very possibly the muddiest person ever to live in the palace. His tutors can usually find him by following the footprints. They lead, most days, either to the gardens or to the kitchens, and only rarely to the schoolroom where he is supposed to be.

### Why, why and why

Alaric asks why about everything. Why the Great Bell rings only for a crown. Why beetles have six legs and spiders eight. Why the cook sings to bread but shouts at soup. Why some envoys want the windows open and others want them shut. The remarkable thing is not the asking but that he remembers every answer, word for word, along with who gave it and whether they looked as if they believed it. His tutors find this exhausting. His father finds it delightful, and has been known to answer a single question about a road with a half-hour lecture and a sketch, which Alaric then keeps.

He collects three things: beetles, keys and rumours. The beetles live in a row of jars on his windowsill, each labelled in large, uneven letters. The keys come from everywhere: old ones from the bottoms of drawers, rusted ones dug out of flowerbeds, one that Cuthbert swears used to open a larder nobody can now find. He has never yet found the locks that most of them fit, and he is certain this is only a matter of time. The rumours he keeps in his head, and he brings the best of them to his mother along with the best of the beetles. Queen Aveline takes both seriously, and Alaric has noticed that she sometimes acts on the rumours.

### Friends in the garden and on the stairs

His two great friends are Godwin and Peterkin. Godwin, the old gardener, has tended the palace gardens since the old king's day, and he lets Alaric dig, water and ask questions as long as he is gentle with the roses. Godwin taught him which beetles help a garden and which ones eat it, and lately the two of them have been watching the wild bees, which Godwin says have turned mean this year. Alaric wants to know why, and for once nobody can tell him.

Peterkin, the palace page, is a little older and never walks anywhere. When he is not carrying messages, he and Alaric race the clock tower bells from the cellars to the roof, or take turns listening at doors in the name of practice. Peterkin is the only person Alaric has told about the passage.

### The secret passage

Alaric is sure there is a secret passage behind the tapestries in the throne hall. He has evidence: a draught that moves the bottom of one tapestry when every door is shut, a hollow sound when he knocks on one stretch of wall, and a key in his collection that fits nothing else in the palace. Osbert, the steward, who knows where every spoon and every secret is kept, will neither confirm nor deny it, and to Alaric that is the best evidence of all.

### His sister

Alaric adores Elinor and is a little afraid of her. He has noticed that she is gone from her room some mornings before even Peterkin is awake, and she has told him she goes riding. He believes her, mostly. He has filed it away with everything else.

### What he wants and fears

Alaric wants to know things, all things, preferably first. He fears very little except being told he is too young to be told, and the nights when his mother does not sleep, which he has noticed too.

A quest might begin with one of his keys turning out to fit something important, or with a rumour he picked up in the kitchens that nobody else has heard yet.
